newsitem.title: CHINA: Sole survivor of China's Gang of Four free.
newsitem.headline: Sole survivor of China's Gang of Four free.

text.p: Two decades after Mao Zedong's chief bodyguard carried out the sensational arrest of Mao's widow and the three other members of her notorious "Gang of Four," the sole survivor was officially free on Sunday.

Yao Wenyuan, 64, has officially completed his 20-year prison term -- 20 years to the day since one of the most sensational moments in the power struggles in China's Communist Party ended a decade of ultra-leftist fervour whipped up by Mao's wife, Jiang Qing.
Chinese sources said Yao has been effectively at liberty since 1994, living in utmost secrecy in his hometown of Shanghai.
If the experience of lesser members of the gang is anything to judge by, Yao can expect to spend the remaining years of his life under tight surveillance and in deep obscurity.

Chinese official media have kept silent on the 20th anniversary of the overthrow of the Gang of Four by the chief of Chairman Mao's palace security staff which came just one month after the death of the Great Helmsman removed their main support.
The issue of their guilt and close links to Mao -- who is still officially revered -- is one that embarrasses communist officialdom and is relegated to the darkest corners.

For example, a former head of the Shanghai military region and an associate of the Gang of Four was released from prison last year, was banned from returning to Shanghai and ordered to return to his ancestral village in neighbouring Jiangsu province.
Even his Chinese visitors and old friends are screened while contact with outsiders would be impossible.
Such is almost certain to be the fate of Yao Wenyuan, who received the most lenient sentence of the four -- 20 years for counter-revolutionary, or subversive, crimes.

Jiang Qing, leader of the Gang of Four that wielded supreme power during the bloody Cultural Revolution, was sentenced to death with a two-year reprieve in 1981 for the deaths of tens of thousands. She never repented, but her sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.
The former Shanghai starlet, dubbed a witch by state media after her downfall, hanged herself in Beijing in May 1991.
Zhang Chunqiao received a suspended death sentence after refusing to utter a single word during the two-month trial. He died in 1991, according to the Encyclopedia of the People's Republic of China.
The fourth and youngest gang member, Wang Hongwen, died of liver cancer in a Beijing hospital in 1992 while serving a life sentence.
The Justice Ministry, which is responsible for convicts, declined to comment on Yao's whereabouts or when his jail term was due to end. Police and courts also refused to comment.

The former member of the powerful party Politburo, heavily built, round-faced and balding when last seen in public at his 1980-81 trial, is deprived of his political rights for the next five years. That means he cannot meet foreign reporters or publish articles.

Yao has been spending his days wielding the pen that wrote his rise to power. He is writing a book and studying Chinese history since his release on medical parole two years ago, Chinese sources said.
Yao first caught Mao's eye as a writer and propaganda official in Shanghai, and he penned the article that effectively launched the fury of the Cultural Revolution.
"He left nothing but a bad impression," said Ai Mo, 79, who was editor-in-chief of the Guangming Daily -- the newspaper of intellectuals -- during the Cultural Revolution.
"He was a tool ... He used his pen to purge intellectuals," said Xu Youyu, an expert on the Cultural Revolution. "He has no role whatsoever to play in today's society."
Many still dread the Gang of Four and avoid mentioning the four people blamed for the turmoil that stirred up tens of millions of Red Guards and destroyed millions of lives.
"I was appointed by the Supreme Court ... I was not hired by him," Han Xuezhang, one of Yao's two defence lawyers, said by telephone from Shanghai. "I don't have any contact with him."
